terminal.description: A shell in your workspace where try.js starts your API on a free port and sends it a few requests.

tasks.title: Send JSON responses
tasks.description:
Implement `sendJson(res, status, body)` in `src/respond.js`. Every route in this API will answer through it.

It writes one complete response:

- the status code is `status`
- the `content-type` header is `application/json; charset=utf-8`
- the `content-length` header is the size of the JSON text in **bytes**
- the body is `body` turned into JSON text, and the response is ended

The check starts a small server that calls your `sendJson` with different statuses and bodies, including one with letters like `ø` and `é`, and reads what a real client receives.
nextSteps: Turn `body` into JSON text first and keep it in a variable.
Write the status and both headers.
End the response with the text.
Press Check. The routes come next, so `node try.js` still shows errors for now.
hints: A response is three things: a status line, headers and a body. `res.writeHead` sets the first two at once.
`'ø'.length` is 1, but it takes 2 bytes on the wire. Node has a helper on `Buffer` that measures a string in bytes.
Call `res.writeHead(status, { ... })` with the two headers, using `Buffer.byteLength(text)` for the length, then `res.end(text)`.

tasks.title: Answer the first routes
tasks.description:
Implement `handleRequest(req, res)` in `src/app.js` so it answers two routes:

- `GET /health` answers `200` with `{ "status": "ok" }`
- `GET /boats` answers `200` with the `fleet` array from `src/fleet.js`, unchanged

Use `sendJson` for both. `req.url` includes the query string, so `GET /boats?available=true` must reach the same route as `GET /boats`.

The check starts your app with `createApp()` on a free port and sends real requests to it.
nextSteps: Read the path out of `req.url` without the query string.
Keep your routes in one object keyed by path, then by method.
Look up the handler for this request and call it.
Run `node try.js` and look at the first two answers.
hints: `req.method` and `req.url` are all you need to pick a route. Print them once to see what they hold.
`new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost')` gives you a `pathname` without the query string.
A table like `{ '/health': { GET: (req, res) => ... } }` makes the lookup two steps: the path, then the method.

tasks.title: Say no clearly
tasks.description:
Make `handleRequest` answer requests it cannot serve, as JSON:

- a path with no route answers `404` with `{ "error": { "code": "not_found", "message": "..." } }`
- a path that exists but not for this method (for example `POST /health`) answers `405` with `{ "error": { "code": "method_not_allowed", "message": "..." } }` and an `allow` header listing the methods that path accepts, such as `GET`

The message is a short sentence for a developer; the check only needs it to be a non-empty string.
nextSteps: Handle the case where no route matches the path.
Then handle the case where the path matches but the method does not.
Build the `allow` header from the methods the route has.
Run `node try.js` and compare the last two answers.
hints: There are two different ways a lookup can miss here. Each one gets its own status.
404 means the thing is not there. 405 means it is there but cannot be used that way.
`Object.keys(route).join(', ')` lists the methods a route has. Set it with `res.setHeader('allow', ...)` before you call sendJson.
